title: India's Economy Grows 7.8% in April-June, Beating All Forecasts
excerpt: GDP growth in Q1 FY2027 comfortably surpassed the 7.1% consensus and the RBI's 7% projection, driven by a surge in manufacturing and investment activity.
body:
• India's GDP grew 7.8% in Q1 FY2027 (April-June), comfortably beating the Reuters consensus of 7.1% and the RBI's 7% projection.
  • Manufacturing expanded 9.2% and financial services surged 12.1%, while gross value added — a measure of underlying activity — grew 8.2%.
  • Investment rose nearly 12% and personal consumption grew 7.1%, driven by GST and income tax cuts.
  • Economists are revising full-year growth forecasts upward to 7%, which would mark India's fourth consecutive year of above-7% growth.

India's economy expanded 7.8% in the April-June quarter, government data released Monday showed, comfortably beating market expectations and reinforcing the country's position as the world's fastest-growing major economy even as the six-month-old West Asia conflict creates persistent headwinds.

The growth figure was well above the 7.1% median forecast in a Reuters poll of 58 economists and the Reserve Bank of India's projection of 7%, though it marked a moderation from the revised 8.6% expansion recorded in the January-March quarter.

Manufacturing and Investment Lead

A surge in manufacturing and investment drove the outperformance. The manufacturing sector grew 9.2%, up from 8.3% a year earlier, while the financial services sector expanded 12.1% compared with 8.8%, fueled by the strongest loan growth in over a decade — 18.3% at the end of the June quarter, according to the RBI's August bulletin.

Gross value added, which strips out the volatile effects of indirect taxes and subsidies to measure underlying economic activity, grew 8.2%. Personal consumption rose 7.1% and investment expanded nearly 12%.

"The surprise is more meaningful than the headline suggests: the run-up to the release was marked by expectations of a slowdown on weak early-monsoon rains and softening services indicators."

— Sujan Hajra, Chief Economist, Anand Rathi Financial Services

Resilience Despite Global Headwinds

The numbers are notable given the backdrop. The West Asia conflict, now six months old, has pushed up energy prices and weakened the rupee by more than 6% against the dollar this year. Despite these pressures, goods and services tax cuts and income tax reductions implemented earlier in the year have supported consumer demand.

"Input cost pressures due to the West Asia conflict were offset by higher volume growth with sectors like manufacturing and electricity, gas growing by close to 9%," said Sakshi Gupta, principal economist at HDFC Bank, according to Reuters. She revised her full-year growth forecast to 7% from 6.8%.

Capital formation climbed to 34.3% in nominal terms, up from 31.4% a year ago, reflecting both public and private expenditure. Bank of Baroda Chief Economist Madan Sabnavis noted this involved "data centres and power besides metals" on the private side.

Risks on the Horizon

While the strong print is encouraging, economists flagged potential headwinds in coming quarters. The uneven monsoon could weigh on agricultural output, and the persistence of high oil prices remains a risk. Private investment, though showing signs of a nascent recovery, has yet to broaden decisively.

"The key risks are now less about a softer domestic story and more about the persistence of high oil prices, rupee weakness and tighter global financial conditions," said Radhika Rao, senior economist at DBS Bank.

Economists in the Reuters poll forecast growth to moderate to 6.6% in the current quarter and average 6.7% for the full fiscal year, in line with RBI projections. But the strong Q1 print has prompted several forecasters to nudge their full-year estimates upward.

What It Means for Investors

The data signals a domestic demand story that remains more resilient than feared. India's strong growth run — potentially the fourth consecutive year above 7% — could support equity markets and attract portfolio inflows, though currency depreciation and elevated oil prices remain drags on returns. The RBI's monetary policy trajectory will be closely watched as policymakers balance growth momentum against inflation and external risks.
